:::{#def-differentiable}
#### Differentiable function

A function $f$ is **differentiable at** $x = c$ if the limit

$$f'(c) \eqdef \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h}$$

exists and is finite.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 2.1, p. 100]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-differentiable-on}
#### Differentiable on an interval

A function $f$ is **differentiable on** an interval
if it is differentiable (@def-differentiable) at every interior point of the interval;
at a closed endpoint, the appropriate one-sided derivative is used.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 2.1, p. 100]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-continuous}
#### Continuous function

A function $f$ is **continuous at** $x = c$ if all three conditions hold:

1. $f(c)$ is defined,
2. $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ exists, and
3. $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 1.4, p. 73]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-continuous-on}
#### Continuous on a closed interval

A function $f$ is **continuous on** a closed interval $[a, b]$
if all three conditions hold:

1. $f$ is continuous (@def-continuous) at every point of the open interval $(a, b)$,
2. $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$, and
3. $\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 1.4, p. 73]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-continuous-on-sqrt}
#### Continuity on $[0, 1]$ uses one-sided limits at the endpoints

Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$, defined for $x \ge 0$.
Because $f$ is undefined for $x < 0$,
only the right-hand limit of $f$ at $0$ makes sense,
and @def-continuous-on asks only for that one-sided limit at the endpoint $0$.
Here $f$ is continuous at every point of $(0, 1)$,
$\lim_{x \to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0 = f(0)$,
and $\lim_{x \to 1^-} \sqrt{x} = 1 = f(1)$,
so $f$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$ (@def-continuous-on).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-partition}
#### Partition of an interval

A **partition** $\mathcal{P}$ of a closed interval $[a, b]$
is a finite list of points

$$a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b.$$

It splits $[a, b]$ into the $n$ subintervals $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$,
of widths $\Delta x_i \eqdef x_i - x_{i-1}$,
and its **mesh** is the largest width,
$\|\mathcal{P}\| \eqdef \max_i \Delta x_i$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-partition}
#### A partition of $[0, 1]$

The points $0 < 0.25 < 0.5 < 1$ form a partition of $[0, 1]$
with $n = 3$ subintervals,
of widths $\Delta x_1 = 0.25$, $\Delta x_2 = 0.25$, and $\Delta x_3 = 0.5$,
so its mesh is $0.5$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-riemann-integral}
#### Riemann integral

Let $f$ be a bounded function on $[a, b]$.
For each partition $\mathcal{P}$ of $[a, b]$ (@def-partition),
choose a sample point $x_i^*$ in each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$.
The **Riemann integral** of $f$ over $[a, b]$ is the limit

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \eqdef \lim_{\|\mathcal{P}\| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x_i,$$

when that limit exists and has the same value
for every choice of the partitions and of the sample points $x_i^*$.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3, p. 272]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-integrable}
#### Riemann integrable

A bounded function $f$ is **Riemann integrable on** $[a, b]$
if its Riemann integral (@def-riemann-integral) over $[a, b]$
exists and is finite.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 4.3, p. 272]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

<!-- This id predates the reframing that made the general-partition form
@def-riemann-integral; it is kept so links to it keep working. -->

:::{#def-integrable-general}
#### Equal-width Riemann sum

For a bounded function $f$ on $[a, b]$ and a positive integer $n$,
split $[a, b]$ into $n$ subintervals of equal width
$\Delta x \eqdef (b - a)/n$,
and let $x_i^*$ be any point in the $i$-th subinterval.
The **equal-width Riemann sum** is

$$S_n \eqdef \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x.$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-equal-width-sum}
#### An equal-width Riemann sum

Let $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, with $n = 2$,
so $\Delta x = 1/2$,
and take each sample point at the right end of its subinterval:
$x_1^* = \frac{1}{2}$ and $x_2^* = 1$.
Then

$$
\ba
S_2
&= f\paren{\tfrac{1}{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{2} + f(1) \cd \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(equal-width Riemann sum with } n = 2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{4} \cd \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 \cd \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(evaluate } f(x) = x^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{5}{8}
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::
